questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is studying the mechanism of spironolactone. The drug binds the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor in collecting duct principal cells. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which spironolactone produces its renal effects?
choices: Competitive antagonism of the mineralocorticoid receptor in collecting duct principal cells, preventing aldosterone-driven transcription of ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase. Net effect: decreased Na+ reabsorption (mild natriuresis), decreased K+ secretion (potassium-sparing), and decreased downstream H+ secretion at α-intercalated cells. Onset is slow (days) because the effect requires turnover of pre-existing transporter protein
Direct inhibition of NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
Direct inhibition of NCC in the early DCT
Direct inhibition of ENaC in the apical membrane
Inhibition of the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
explanations: Correct. Spironolactone is a competitive antagonist of the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in collecting duct principal cells. By blocking aldosterone binding, it prevents transcriptional upregulation of ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase. The net effects are decreased Na+ reabsorption (mild natriuresis), decreased K+ secretion (potassium-sparing), and decreased H+ secretion at adjacent α-intercalated cells (which depend on the lumen-negative voltage created by ENaC-mediated Na+ entry). Onset is slow — typically 2–4 days — because the existing pool of ENaC/ROMK proteins must be turned over before the steroid-receptor blockade is fully manifest.
Incorrect. NKCC2 inhibition is the loop diuretic mechanism.
Incorrect. NCC inhibition is the thiazide mechanism.
Incorrect. Direct ENaC inhibition is the mechanism of amiloride and triamterene — not spironolactone.
Incorrect. Spironolactone does not directly inhibit Na+/K+-ATPase.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with HFrEF is on amiloride 5 mg daily. Amiloride binds and blocks the apical epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) directly. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which amiloride produces its renal effects?
choices: Competitive antagonism of the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor

Direct blockade of ENaC in the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells, reducing Na+ entry from the lumen. Reduced Na+ entry diminishes the lumen-negative transepithelial voltage that drives K+ secretion via apical ROMK and H+ secretion at α-intercalated cells. Net effect: mild natriuresis, K+-sparing, less H+ secretion. Onset is rapid (hours), unlike spironolactone
Inhibition of NCC in the early distal convoluted tubule
Inhibition of basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase
explanations: Incorrect. MR antagonism is the spironolactone/eplerenone mechanism — distinct from direct ENaC blockade.

Correct. Amiloride and triamterene directly block apical ENaC in collecting duct principal cells, reducing Na+ entry from the tubular lumen into the cell. With less Na+ entering through ENaC, the lumen-negative transepithelial voltage falls — and this voltage is the principal driving force for K+ secretion through apical ROMK and for H+ secretion at adjacent α-intercalated cells. The net effect is mild natriuresis, K+-sparing, and reduced acid excretion. Onset is rapid (hours, since the channel is blocked directly), unlike spironolactone (days, since transcription is the target).
Incorrect. NCC inhibition is the thiazide mechanism.
Incorrect. Amiloride does not inhibit Na+/K+-ATPase.
Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition is the acetazolamide mechanism.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with HFrEF developed gynecomastia and decreased libido after 6 months on spironolactone. His clinician switches him to eplerenone. Which row in the table best characterizes spironolactone (compared with eplerenone)?

rows: Once or twice daily; long half-life via active metabolite (canrenone)
Spironolactone is more selective than eplerenone

choices: A
B
C
D
E
explanations: Correct. Spironolactone is a non-selective steroid that binds not only the mineralocorticoid receptor but also androgen and progesterone receptors. The antiandrogenic effects include gynecomastia, decreased libido, and impotence in men, and menstrual irregularities and breast tenderness in women. Spironolactone is a prodrug; its active metabolite canrenone has a long half-life supporting once- or twice-daily dosing. Eplerenone (row B) is highly MR-selective with minimal antiandrogen / antiprogesterone activity but shorter half-life requiring BID dosing.
Incorrect. This is the eplerenone profile, not spironolactone.
Incorrect. The two drugs differ in selectivity and hormonal effects; they are not identical.
Incorrect. Eplerenone is MORE selective than spironolactone, not the reverse.
Incorrect. The two drugs have measurable differences in selectivity, hormonal effects, and dosing.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with thiazide-induced hypokalemia is started on triamterene 50 mg daily as a K+-sparing addition. He develops a small kidney stone 2 years later, and stone analysis identifies the drug. Which of the following best characterizes triamterene compared with amiloride?
choices: Triamterene and amiloride are essentially identical in pharmacology
Triamterene has a longer half-life than amiloride

Triamterene is metabolized to a 7-O-sulfate metabolite that can crystallize and form triamterene-containing kidney stones (a rare but recognized adverse effect not seen with amiloride). Both directly block ENaC in collecting duct principal cells; amiloride is more potent on a mg basis (5–10 mg dose vs triamterene 50–100 mg). Triamterene also has weak folate antagonist activity
Triamterene blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor
Triamterene acts at NCC in the DCT
explanations: Incorrect. The two have important pharmacologic differences.
Incorrect. Amiloride has a LONGER half-life than triamterene.

Correct. Both amiloride and triamterene directly block apical ENaC in collecting duct principal cells, but they differ pharmacologically. Triamterene is metabolized to a 7-O-sulfate metabolite that can crystallize in tubular fluid, occasionally forming triamterene-containing kidney stones. Amiloride is not stone-forming. Amiloride is more potent per mg (5–10 mg dose vs triamterene 50–100 mg). Both are typically used in combination products with thiazides (HCTZ + triamterene = Dyazide; HCTZ + amiloride). Triamterene also has weak folate antagonist activity.
Incorrect. Triamterene blocks ENaC directly, not the MR.
Incorrect. Triamterene acts at ENaC, not NCC.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old researcher is reviewing the effects of aldosterone on the cortical collecting duct, illustrated below. The diagram shows the principal cell with apical ENaC, ROMK, and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, with aldosterone activating the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor. Where in this pathway does spironolactone act, and where does amiloride act?
questions.diagram:
Cortical collecting duct principal cell — aldosterone signaling
Aldosterone → cytosolic MR ← × blocked by spironolactone / eplerenone
↓ (gene transcription)
Apical: ENaC (Na+ entry) ← × blocked directly by amiloride / triamterene
Apical: ROMK (K+ exit, driven by lumen-negative voltage)
Basolateral: Na+/K+-ATPase (Na+ exit, K+ entry)
Adjacent α-intercalated cells: H+-ATPase (H+ exit, driven by lumen-negative voltage)
choices: Spironolactone blocks ENaC; amiloride blocks the MR
Spironolactone blocks NKCC2; amiloride blocks ENaC
Spironolactone blocks NCC; amiloride blocks the MR

Spironolactone competitively antagonizes the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor (preventing aldosterone-driven transcription of ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase). Amiloride directly blocks ENaC in the apical membrane (independent of aldosterone signaling). Both reduce K+ secretion downstream by reducing the lumen-negative transepithelial voltage, but they act at different points in the pathway. This is why amiloride works in Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC, downstream of MR) while spironolactone does not
Both drugs block the same target — apical ENaC
explanations: Incorrect. The roles are reversed; spironolactone blocks the MR, amiloride blocks ENaC.
Incorrect. Spironolactone does not block NKCC2.
Incorrect. Spironolactone does not block NCC.

Correct. Spironolactone (and eplerenone) competitively antagonize the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor, preventing aldosterone-driven transcription of ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase. Amiloride (and triamterene) directly block ENaC in the apical membrane. Both reduce the lumen-negative transepithelial voltage that drives K+ secretion through ROMK and H+ secretion at adjacent α-intercalated cells. The key clinical distinction: in Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC) the lesion is DOWNSTREAM of the MR, so spironolactone fails — amiloride is the appropriate K+-sparing agent.
Incorrect. The two drugs target different molecules along the same pathway.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with HFrEF (NYHA class III, EF 25%) on optimal ACE inhibitor and β-blocker therapy still has symptoms. The team adds spironolactone 25 mg daily. The Randomized Aldactone Evaluation Study (RALES) showed that spironolactone added to standard HF therapy reduces what outcome in HFrEF patients?
choices: Increases HF hospitalizations and mortality
Reduces blood pressure but does not affect mortality
Reduces LV ejection fraction over time
Has no effect on outcomes

Reduces all-cause mortality (~30% relative reduction in RALES) and HF hospitalizations in NYHA class III/IV HFrEF on background ACE inhibitor and β-blocker therapy. The mortality benefit reflects mineralocorticoid-receptor-mediated cardiac and vascular fibrosis prevention, beyond simple K+-sparing diuretic effect. Mineralocorticoid antagonists (spironolactone or eplerenone) are now class I therapy for HFrEF in patients with eGFR ≥30 and K+ ≤5.0
explanations: Incorrect. Spironolactone REDUCES mortality and HF hospitalizations in HFrEF.
Incorrect. Spironolactone has substantial outcome benefits beyond BP reduction.
Incorrect. Spironolactone may IMPROVE LV function over time.
Incorrect. Spironolactone has substantial mortality and morbidity benefits.

Correct. RALES (1999) demonstrated a ~30% relative reduction in all-cause mortality with spironolactone 25 mg daily added to background ACE inhibitor and β-blocker therapy in NYHA class III/IV HFrEF. Subsequent trials extended these findings: EPHESUS (2003) showed eplerenone reduces mortality post-MI with HF/diabetes; EMPHASIS-HF (2011) showed eplerenone reduces mortality in NYHA class II HFrEF. The benefit is thought to reflect MR-mediated reduction in cardiac and vascular fibrosis (beyond simple K+-sparing diuretic effect). Mineralocorticoid antagonists are guideline-directed (class I) therapy for HFrEF in patients with eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m² and serum K+ ≤5.0; close monitoring of K+ and renal function is essential.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has an acute MI 3 weeks ago and now has NYHA class II HFrEF (EF 30%). Her clinician adds eplerenone 25 mg daily. The EPHESUS trial established the role of eplerenone post-MI. Which of the following best characterizes the EPHESUS findings?
choices: Eplerenone reduces all-cause mortality and CV mortality in patients with HF (EF ≤40%) post-MI, particularly when started 3–14 days after MI; benefits are independent of background ACE inhibitor and β-blocker therapy. Subsequent EMPHASIS-HF trial extended benefit to chronic NYHA class II HFrEF
Eplerenone increases mortality post-MI
Eplerenone has no effect post-MI
Eplerenone is contraindicated post-MI
Eplerenone is a placebo control
explanations: Correct. EPHESUS (2003) randomized ~6,600 patients with acute MI complicated by HF (EF ≤40%) and either HF symptoms or diabetes to eplerenone vs placebo, started 3–14 days post-MI. Eplerenone reduced all-cause mortality by ~15% and CV mortality similarly, with benefit emerging within 30 days. Adding to ACE inhibitor and β-blocker therapy. EPHESUS established eplerenone post-MI for HFrEF. EMPHASIS-HF (2011) extended benefit to chronic NYHA class II HFrEF (EF ≤30 or 35 with previous CV hospitalization).
Incorrect. EPHESUS showed mortality REDUCTION.
Incorrect. EPHESUS showed substantial outcome benefit.
Incorrect. Eplerenone is INDICATED post-MI with HFrEF; not contraindicated.
Incorrect. Eplerenone is the active intervention in EPHESUS.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and tense ascites is being started on diuretic therapy. The clinician chooses combination therapy with spironolactone 100 mg + furosemide 40 mg orally daily. Which of the following best explains why spironolactone is preferred as the first-line diuretic in cirrhotic ascites?
choices: Spironolactone produces faster diuresis than other diuretics in cirrhosis

Cirrhotic ascites is principally driven by aldosterone excess: splanchnic vasodilation reduces effective arterial volume, activating RAAS; the resulting high aldosterone drives renal Na+ retention. Spironolactone directly antagonizes this central pathophysiologic mechanism. Combined with furosemide in 100:40 ratio, the regimen also balances K+ effects (spironolactone's K+-sparing action offsets furosemide's K+-wasting). AASLD guidelines recommend this combination
Spironolactone is the cheapest diuretic
Spironolactone is the only diuretic safe in cirrhosis
Spironolactone increases serum albumin
explanations: Incorrect. Spironolactone's onset is SLOW (days), not faster than other diuretics. The choice is based on mechanism, not speed.

Correct. Cirrhotic ascites pathophysiology centers on aldosterone excess: splanchnic vasodilation (driven by NO, glucagon, and other mediators) reduces effective arterial volume, activating RAAS. The resulting high aldosterone drives intense renal Na+ retention. Spironolactone directly antagonizes the MR and is therefore mechanism-matched first-line therapy. Combination with furosemide (100:40 ratio: spironolactone 100 mg + furosemide 40 mg) provides additional natriuresis while balancing K+ effects (spironolactone-induced K+ retention offsets furosemide-induced K+ loss). AASLD guidelines support this combination. Sodium restriction (≤2 g/day) is essential. Tense or refractory ascites may require large-volume paracentesis with albumin or TIPS.
Incorrect. Spironolactone is not chosen for cost reasons.
Incorrect. Other diuretics (loop) are widely used in cirrhosis when combined appropriately.
Incorrect. Spironolactone does not raise serum albumin.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension on amlodipine + lisinopril + chlorthalidone still has BP 160/95 (above goal). She is adherent and there are no secondary causes. The PATHWAY-2 trial established the optimal 4th-line agent for resistant hypertension. Which of the following is the recommended 4th-line agent based on this trial?
choices: Hydralazine

Spironolactone (PATHWAY-2 trial, 2015) — added to background ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide produced significantly greater BP reduction than bisoprolol or doxazosin in patients with resistant hypertension. The mechanism reflects the often-unrecognized aldosterone contribution to apparent treatment-resistant hypertension; many such patients have biochemical evidence of aldosterone excess
Methyldopa
Clonidine
Minoxidil
explanations: Incorrect. Hydralazine is reserved for refractory or specific cases (HF in pregnancy or African-Americans with HF); not the optimal 4th-line agent for resistant HTN.

Correct. PATHWAY-2 (Williams et al, Lancet 2015) randomized patients with resistant hypertension on three-drug therapy (ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide) to spironolactone, bisoprolol, doxazosin, or placebo as a 4th agent. Spironolactone produced greater BP reduction than bisoprolol or doxazosin, with the magnitude of response correlating inversely with renin levels (low-renin patients had greater BP fall — supporting an underlying aldosterone-driven mechanism). The trial established spironolactone as the recommended 4th-line agent for resistant HTN. Mechanism: many patients with apparently resistant HTN have biochemical primary or secondary aldosterone excess, even when clinical screening is negative.
Incorrect. Methyldopa is principally used in pregnancy.
Incorrect. Clonidine has rebound hypertension on withdrawal and is not preferred 4th-line.
Incorrect. Minoxidil is used in severe refractory cases but is not first-line 4th-step therapy.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with newly diagnosed Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism from a unilateral adrenal adenoma) is being prepared for laparoscopic adrenalectomy. The team starts spironolactone 25 mg daily preoperatively. Which of the following best explains the role of spironolactone in preoperative management?
choices: Spironolactone shrinks the adrenal adenoma
Spironolactone is the standard surgical anesthetic premedication
Spironolactone improves wound healing

Spironolactone normalizes BP and corrects hypokalemia preoperatively (by antagonizing aldosterone's effects on principal cells); 4–8 weeks of therapy allows resolution of suppressed contralateral aldosterone secretion, reducing the risk of postoperative hyperkalemia (otherwise, the adrenal contralateral to the adenoma may be slow to resume aldosterone production)
Spironolactone has no role preoperatively
explanations: Incorrect. Spironolactone does not shrink the adenoma.
Incorrect. Spironolactone is not an anesthetic.
Incorrect. Spironolactone does not affect wound healing.

Correct. Preoperative spironolactone (or eplerenone) in primary hyperaldosteronism serves two purposes: (1) normalizing blood pressure and correcting hypokalemia (and metabolic alkalosis) by antagonizing the elevated aldosterone — improving the patient's perioperative status; (2) allowing 4–8 weeks of suppression of aldosterone-driven Na+ retention, which 'lifts' the chronic suppression of renin and aldosterone in the CONTRALATERAL adrenal gland. Without this preparation, the contralateral adrenal may be sluggish to resume aldosterone production after the affected adrenal is removed, risking postoperative hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. Medical management with spironolactone is also an alternative to surgery for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, where surgery is less curative.
Incorrect. Spironolactone has a clear preoperative role in primary hyperaldosteronism.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC mutation) has hypertension and hypokalemia. His clinician is choosing between spironolactone and amiloride. Which row in the table best describes the comparison of mechanism and effectiveness in Liddle syndrome?

rows: No (lesion is downstream of the MR)

choices: A
B
C
D
E
explanations: Incorrect. This describes spironolactone/eplerenone (MR antagonists). MR antagonists DO NOT WORK in Liddle syndrome because the gain-of-function ENaC mutation is DOWNSTREAM of the MR — the channel is constitutively active even without aldosterone signaling.

Correct. Amiloride (and triamterene) directly block apical ENaC, including the gain-of-function ENaC mutant in Liddle syndrome. Direct ENaC blockade bypasses the (already-disabled) aldosterone signaling pathway. Liddle is one of the few clinical scenarios where ENaC blockers are clearly superior to MR antagonists. Treatment dramatically improves blood pressure and corrects hypokalemia. Amiloride lacks antiandrogen effects.
Incorrect. NCC blockade (thiazide) does not target the underlying ENaC defect.
Incorrect. NKCC2 blockade (loop) does not target the underlying ENaC defect.
Incorrect. The two drug classes have measurable differences in Liddle syndrome treatment.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with severe hypertension at age 22, hypokalemia, suppressed plasma renin, suppressed aldosterone, and a strong family history of premature renal failure. Genetic testing confirms a gain-of-function mutation in the β-subunit of ENaC (Liddle syndrome). His clinician starts him on spironolactone, but BP remains uncontrolled at 175/108. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Continue spironolactone at higher dose
Add hydrochlorothiazide
Add eplerenone instead of spironolactone
Add an ACE inhibitor

Switch from spironolactone to amiloride (or triamterene), which DIRECTLY blocks the constitutively active ENaC channel — bypassing the (disabled) mineralocorticoid receptor signaling that spironolactone targets. Spironolactone is INEFFECTIVE in Liddle syndrome because the gain-of-function mutation makes ENaC active independent of aldosterone-driven transcription
explanations: Incorrect. Spironolactone is ineffective in Liddle syndrome regardless of dose; the lesion is downstream of the MR.
Incorrect. Thiazides may help BP but do not address the underlying ENaC defect; addition of a direct ENaC blocker is mechanism-matched.
Incorrect. Eplerenone is also an MR antagonist; it shares spironolactone's failure mode in Liddle.
Incorrect. ACE inhibitors target a system upstream of aldosterone, but Liddle does NOT depend on aldosterone signaling — the ENaC is constitutively active.

Correct. Liddle syndrome is caused by gain-of-function mutations in ENaC (deletion of a PY motif that normally targets ENaC for ubiquitin-mediated degradation by Nedd4). The mutant channel is constitutively active, producing Na+ retention, K+ secretion, and H+ secretion — without need for aldosterone signaling. Plasma renin and aldosterone are SUPPRESSED (the volume expansion provides feedback). Spironolactone (MR antagonist) is INEFFECTIVE because it acts upstream of the disease-causing lesion. Direct ENaC blockade with amiloride or triamterene bypasses the broken MR pathway and corrects BP and electrolytes. This is one of the few clinical scenarios where mechanism dictates a clear choice between K+-sparing diuretic classes.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with PCOS and hirsutism is started on spironolactone 100 mg daily for cosmetic improvement of unwanted facial hair. Within 6 months her hirsutism has improved noticeably. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of spironolactone's effect on hirsutism?
choices: Spironolactone has antiandrogenic activity through competitive binding at peripheral androgen receptors and partial inhibition of androgen synthesis (5α-reductase, cytochrome P450 cleavage of cholesterol side chains). Combined with its weak antiprogestogenic effect, this reduces androgen-driven terminal hair growth. Used at 50–200 mg daily in PCOS-related hirsutism (and acne), generally combined with oral contraceptive for greater effect and pregnancy avoidance (spironolactone is teratogenic to male fetuses)
Spironolactone stimulates estrogen receptors directly
Spironolactone is a 5α-reductase inhibitor specifically (like finasteride)
Spironolactone is FDA-indicated for hirsutism
Spironolactone has no effect on hirsutism
explanations: Correct. Spironolactone has multiple antiandrogenic effects: (1) competitive binding at peripheral androgen receptors blocks dihydrotestosterone from reaching its target; (2) partial inhibition of androgen synthesis (interferes with cytochrome P450 cleavage of cholesterol side chains, reducing testosterone production); (3) weak inhibition of 5α-reductase. Combined, these reduce androgen-driven terminal hair growth and sebum production. Used at 50–200 mg daily for PCOS-related hirsutism and acne; usually combined with combined oral contraceptive (which suppresses ovarian androgen production AND prevents pregnancy, since spironolactone is teratogenic to male fetuses). Effects on hair are seen over 4–6 months. Off-label use but well-established.
Incorrect. Spironolactone does not stimulate estrogen receptors directly.
Incorrect. Finasteride is a specific 5α-reductase inhibitor; spironolactone has only weak inhibitory activity at this enzyme.
Incorrect. The hirsutism use is off-label (not FDA-indicated), although well-established.
Incorrect. Spironolactone DOES reduce hirsutism via antiandrogen mechanisms.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with HFrEF is on lisinopril and spironolactone. She started ibuprofen for osteoarthritis 1 week ago. She presents with weakness, palpitations, and ECG showing peaked T waves and widened QRS. Laboratory studies are shown.

labs.name: ECG
labs.value: Peaked T waves, widened QRS, flattened P waves

choices: Acute tumor lysis syndrome

Combined ACE inhibitor + spironolactone + NSAID effect: lisinopril reduces angiotensin II → reduced aldosterone; spironolactone blocks the MR; ibuprofen reduces prostaglandin-mediated afferent vasodilation, lowering GFR (reducing distal Na+ delivery and impairing distal K+ secretion). The 'triple whammy' converges on impaired distal K+ secretion, producing severe hyperkalemia. Management: stop offending agents (NSAID first), urgent hyperkalemia treatment (calcium gluconate, insulin/glucose, β2 agonist), and renal support if needed
Acute hemolysis releasing intracellular K+
Type 1 (distal) RTA
Acidosis-mediated cellular K+ shift
explanations: Incorrect. TLS would feature hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia in addition to hyperkalemia.

Correct. The 'triple whammy' of ACE inhibitor (or ARB) + spironolactone (or eplerenone) + NSAID converges on distal K+ secretion: the ACE inhibitor lowers AT II → lowers aldosterone; spironolactone blocks the MR; the NSAID reduces afferent prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation, lowering GFR and reducing distal Na+ delivery. Each impairs K+ secretion individually; together they produce life-threatening hyperkalemia, especially in elderly patients with HF and reduced renal function. Recognition prompts withdrawal of the offending drugs (the NSAID is usually the easiest to stop). Immediate hyperkalemia treatment includes calcium gluconate (membrane stabilization), insulin/glucose (cellular shift), β2 agonist (cellular shift), loop diuretic if intact kidney function, GI cation exchanger, or hemodialysis.
Incorrect. Hemolysis would show indirect hyperbilirubinemia, low haptoglobin, and elevated LDH — not described here.
Incorrect. Type 1 RTA features HYPOkalemia, not hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. The mild HCO3− decrease is far too small to explain a K+ rise from baseline to 7.4.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with HFrEF on spironolactone 25 mg daily has developed gynecomastia and decreased libido after 6 months. His clinician is considering switching to eplerenone. Which of the following best characterizes the difference between the two drugs?
choices: Eplerenone has a longer half-life than spironolactone

Eplerenone is highly mineralocorticoid receptor-selective with minimal binding to androgen and progesterone receptors; gynecomastia, decreased libido, and menstrual irregularities are markedly less common than with spironolactone. The trade-off is shorter half-life requiring twice-daily dosing. Both are equally effective in HF (RALES for spironolactone, EMPHASIS-HF for eplerenone)
Eplerenone is twice as potent as spironolactone
Eplerenone has stronger antiandrogen effects
Eplerenone is administered once weekly
explanations: Incorrect. Eplerenone has a SHORTER half-life than spironolactone (and its active metabolite canrenone), which is why eplerenone typically requires twice-daily dosing.

Correct. Eplerenone was developed as a more selective MR antagonist that preserves K+-sparing effects without the antiandrogen / antiprogesterone side effects of spironolactone. Endocrine adverse effects (gynecomastia, decreased libido, menstrual irregularities) are markedly less common with eplerenone. The trade-off: shorter half-life (BID dosing typically), and slightly higher cost. Both have similar HF mortality benefits (RALES for spironolactone, EPHESUS and EMPHASIS-HF for eplerenone). Switching to eplerenone is appropriate when spironolactone is otherwise effective but causing endocrine intolerance.
Incorrect. Eplerenone is somewhat LESS potent than spironolactone on a mg-for-mg basis (typical doses 25–50 mg vs spironolactone 12.5–50 mg).
Incorrect. Eplerenone has WEAKER antiandrogen effects, not stronger.
Incorrect. Eplerenone is typically given BID, not weekly.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF and CKD has eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m² and serum K+ 5.0 mEq/L. He is on lisinopril and metoprolol succinate. The team considers adding spironolactone for HF mortality benefit. Which of the following best describes the appropriate use of mineralocorticoid antagonists in this clinical scenario?
choices: Add spironolactone immediately at full dose (25–50 mg daily)
Add spironolactone at any dose without monitoring
Add eplerenone 50 mg twice daily without monitoring

Avoid mineralocorticoid antagonists in this patient because of high hyperkalemia risk: eGFR <30 (or <45 with K+ already at upper limit) and K+ ≥5.0 are recognized contraindications. Initiating MR antagonists in this setting risks severe hyperkalemia. Optimization of other HF therapy (diuretics, β-blockers, ARNi, SGLT2 inhibitor) and close monitoring are preferred. If a future improvement in eGFR or K+ occurs, MR antagonist may be reconsidered
Start an ACE inhibitor instead
explanations: Incorrect. eGFR <30 and/or K+ ≥5.0 are recognized contraindications to initiating MR antagonists due to high hyperkalemia risk.
Incorrect. Monitoring is essential when MR antagonists are used.
Incorrect. Eplerenone shares hyperkalemia risk with spironolactone; eGFR/K+ thresholds apply to both.

Correct. Mineralocorticoid antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) are guideline-directed therapy for HFrEF, but their use is limited by hyperkalemia risk. Recommended thresholds for SAFE initiation: eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m² (some guidelines say ≥45) and serum K+ ≤5.0 mEq/L. In this patient with eGFR 28 and K+ at upper limit, MR antagonist initiation risks severe hyperkalemia. Alternative HF strategies: optimize ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan), SGLT2 inhibitor (proven HFrEF benefit even in advanced CKD), β-blocker, diuretics. Monitor renal function and K+ closely; if improvement occurs, MR antagonist can be reconsidered. The new agent finerenone (a non-steroidal MR antagonist) is approved for diabetic CKD and may have a more favorable hyperkalemia profile in this population.
Incorrect. The patient is already on lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man on triamterene 50 mg daily for thiazide-induced hypokalemia presents with right flank pain. Renal ultrasound shows a 6-mm stone in the right kidney. Stone analysis is performed. Which of the following best characterizes triamterene-related kidney stones?
choices: Triamterene stones are uric acid stones (similar to allopurinol-treated)
Triamterene stones are calcium oxalate (caused by hypercalciuria)
Triamterene stones are calcium phosphate from urinary alkalinization
Triamterene stones are struvite (infection-related)

Triamterene is metabolized to a 7-O-sulfate metabolite that can crystallize in tubular fluid, occasionally producing distinctive triamterene-containing kidney stones (rare adverse effect, distinct from amiloride which is not stone-forming). Diagnosis is by stone analysis showing the metabolite. Discontinuation usually prevents recurrence; small stones often pass spontaneously. Patients with previous triamterene stones should avoid the drug
explanations: Incorrect. Uric acid stones are radiolucent and form in acidic urine; not the triamterene mechanism.
Incorrect. Calcium oxalate stones are common but unrelated to triamterene.
Incorrect. Calcium phosphate stones form in alkaline urine; not the triamterene mechanism.
Incorrect. Struvite stones form from urea-splitting bacteria.

Correct. Triamterene undergoes hepatic metabolism to a 7-O-sulfate metabolite, which can crystallize in tubular fluid and form triamterene-containing stones. This is a RARE but RECOGNIZED adverse effect of triamterene; amiloride does not share this risk. Stone analysis can identify the drug-related component. Risk factors: high doses, prolonged therapy, individual susceptibility. Management: discontinue triamterene (small stones often pass; lithotripsy or surgical management for larger stones); patients with previous triamterene stones should avoid the drug. Switching to amiloride is a reasonable alternative.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on long-term lithium develops nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with polyuria of 5 L/day. Her psychiatrist cannot stop lithium. Which of the following K+-sparing diuretics has a specific role in lithium-induced nephrogenic DI?
choices: Amiloride blocks ENaC in the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells. Importantly, amiloride also blocks the reuptake of LITHIUM from the lumen (lithium enters principal cells via ENaC, where it accumulates and disrupts AQP2 trafficking). Blocking ENaC therefore prevents lithium from entering principal cells and partially reverses lithium-induced AQP2 dysfunction. Amiloride is sometimes added in patients who must continue lithium and have NDI; thiazides are also used (paradoxical antidiuresis from volume contraction)
Spironolactone has the same effect as amiloride
Eplerenone is preferred over amiloride for lithium NDI
Triamterene has a unique role in lithium NDI
K+-sparing diuretics have no role in lithium-induced NDI
explanations: Correct. Amiloride has a specific role in lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Lithium enters principal cells through apical ENaC (lithium is a small monovalent cation similar to Na+ and is transported by ENaC and other Na+ channels). Once intracellular, lithium disrupts AQP2 trafficking by inhibiting GSK-3β and other signaling pathways, producing the NDI phenotype. Amiloride blocks ENaC and PREVENTS lithium uptake INTO principal cells — partially reversing the AQP2 dysfunction. Amiloride is therefore used as adjunctive therapy in patients who must continue lithium and have NDI. Thiazide diuretics also help (paradoxical antidiuresis via volume contraction → enhanced proximal water reabsorption → less distal water delivery).
Incorrect. Spironolactone (MR antagonist) does not block apical ENaC; it does not prevent lithium uptake into principal cells.
Incorrect. Eplerenone is also an MR antagonist; it does not have amiloride's specific role.
Incorrect. Triamterene blocks ENaC similarly to amiloride but is generally less convenient (50 mg dose vs 5 mg for amiloride; risk of triamterene stones).
Incorrect. K+-sparing diuretics (specifically amiloride) DO have a role in lithium-induced NDI.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with severe hypertension since age 22, hypokalemia, suppressed plasma renin, and suppressed plasma aldosterone is started on amiloride 10 mg daily. Within 3 weeks his BP normalizes and his hypokalemia resolves. Genetic testing confirms a mutation. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism)

Liddle syndrome — autosomal-dominant gain-of-function mutation in the β or γ subunit of ENaC; constitutive ENaC activity produces Na+ retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, and SUPPRESSED renin and aldosterone (the negative feedback). Direct ENaC blockade (amiloride or triamterene) corrects BP and electrolytes; mineralocorticoid antagonists (spironolactone) are INEFFECTIVE because the lesion is downstream of the MR. The dramatic response to amiloride and the lab profile confirm the diagnosis
Pheochromocytoma
Bartter syndrome
Cushing syndrome
explanations: Incorrect. Conn syndrome features ELEVATED aldosterone with suppressed renin; this patient has BOTH suppressed.

Correct. Liddle syndrome is an autosomal-dominant gain-of-function mutation in the β or γ subunit of ENaC (deletion of a PY motif that normally targets ENaC for ubiquitin-mediated degradation). The mutant ENaC is constitutively active in collecting duct principal cells, producing Na+ retention, K+ secretion, and H+ secretion — without need for aldosterone signaling. Volume expansion suppresses renin AND aldosterone (both are LOW). Phenotype: severe hypertension at young age, hypokalemic alkalosis, suppressed renin/aldosterone, family history. Treatment with amiloride or triamterene (direct ENaC blockade) is dramatically effective; spironolactone fails (downstream lesion). The dramatic response in this patient confirms the diagnosis biochemically; genetic testing confirms it molecularly.
Incorrect. Pheochromocytoma produces episodic hypertension with catecholamine surge.
Incorrect. Bartter features LOW or normal BP and HIGH renin/aldosterone.
Incorrect. Cushing features cortisol excess with characteristic features (moon facies, abdominal obesity, easy bruising).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with HFrEF starts spironolactone 25 mg daily. After 3 days he has had no significant change in symptoms or weight, and he asks why he isn't improving. Which of the following best characterizes the onset of action of spironolactone?
choices: Spironolactone has a rapid onset (hours), so absent response after 3 days suggests it is not working
Spironolactone is a prodrug and ineffective

Spironolactone has a SLOW onset of action (typically 2–4 days for full effect, with some patients requiring 1–2 weeks). The mechanism is transcriptional: the drug must reach the cytosolic MR, prevent aldosterone binding, and the existing pool of ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase proteins must turn over. This is in contrast to amiloride, which directly blocks ENaC with onset within hours. Spironolactone in HF is given for long-term mortality benefit, not acute diuresis
Spironolactone never produces clinical benefit
Spironolactone is contraindicated in HF
explanations: Incorrect. Spironolactone has a SLOW (not rapid) onset; days are expected.
Incorrect. Spironolactone IS a prodrug (active metabolite canrenone), but it is effective once converted.

Correct. Spironolactone has a slow onset of action because it works through transcriptional regulation: by binding the cytosolic MR, it prevents aldosterone-driven transcription of new ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase proteins. The existing pool of these transporters must be turned over before the effect is fully manifest, which takes 2–4 days. Some patients require 1–2 weeks for maximal response. This is fundamentally different from amiloride, which directly blocks the apical ENaC channel with onset within hours. In HF, spironolactone is given for long-term mortality benefit (RALES, EMPHASIS-HF), not for acute diuresis. Acute decompensation is treated with loop diuretics; spironolactone provides chronic background therapy with mortality benefit.
Incorrect. Spironolactone produces important clinical benefit (HF mortality reduction).
Incorrect. Spironolactone is INDICATED in HFrEF (class I therapy).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with hypertension and thiazide-induced hypokalemia is prescribed a combination diuretic product. Which of the following K+-sparing combinations is most commonly used in clinical practice?
choices: Furosemide alone
Spironolactone alone
Mannitol + amiloride

Hydrochlorothiazide + triamterene (Dyazide®, Maxzide®) or hydrochlorothiazide + amiloride (Moduretic®) — combination products that pair the BP-lowering effect of thiazide with K+-sparing partner; used when thiazide alone produces hypokalemia or when the combination's modest synergistic effect is desired. Triamterene-containing products are most common; amiloride-containing products are less expensive but have somewhat fewer combinations available. Spironolactone + HCTZ (Aldactazide®) is less common as a fixed combination
Loop diuretic + spironolactone in 100:40 ratio (used in cirrhotic ascites, but not a single combined product)
explanations: Incorrect. Furosemide alone causes hypokalemia and is not K+-sparing.
Incorrect. Spironolactone alone is K+-sparing but is not the typical single-pill combination for HTN with hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Mannitol + amiloride is not a clinical combination.

Correct. Combination products that pair thiazide with K+-sparing diuretic are widely used in clinical practice, particularly for hypertension when thiazide-induced hypokalemia would otherwise be problematic. Most common: HCTZ + triamterene (Dyazide®, Maxzide®). HCTZ + amiloride (Moduretic®) is also available but less common. HCTZ + spironolactone (Aldactazide®) is less popular as a fixed combination. The advantages of combination products are simplified dosing (single pill), proven efficacy, and cost effectiveness. Limitations include fixed dose ratios that may not suit all patients.
Incorrect. The 100:40 spironolactone:furosemide combination is used in cirrhotic ascites but is generally given as separate medications, not a single combined product.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with mild HFrEF (NYHA class II, EF 30%) on optimal background therapy (ACEi, β-blocker) is being considered for eplerenone. The EMPHASIS-HF trial extended the use of MR antagonists from severe HF (RALES, EPHESUS) to mild HF. Which of the following best characterizes EMPHASIS-HF findings?
choices: Eplerenone REDUCES mortality and HF hospitalization in NYHA class II HFrEF (EF ≤30 or 35 with prior CV hospitalization) on background ACEi/ARB and β-blocker therapy. The findings extended MR antagonist therapy from severe HF (RALES, EPHESUS) to mild HF, supporting their use across the spectrum of HFrEF. Trial stopped early due to clear benefit
Eplerenone has no benefit in mild HF
Eplerenone increases mortality in mild HF
Eplerenone is contraindicated in mild HF
Eplerenone is required only in NYHA class IV HF
explanations: Correct. EMPHASIS-HF (Zannad et al, NEJM 2011) randomized ~2,700 patients with NYHA class II HFrEF (EF ≤30, or 35 with prior CV hospitalization) on background ACEi/ARB and β-blocker therapy to eplerenone vs placebo. The trial was stopped early due to clear benefit: ~37% reduction in CV death or HF hospitalization, ~24% reduction in all-cause mortality. Findings extended MR antagonist mortality benefit from severe HF (RALES at NYHA III/IV; EPHESUS post-MI with HF) to mild chronic HF, supporting their use across the HFrEF spectrum. MR antagonists are now class I therapy for HFrEF in patients with eGFR ≥30 and K+ ≤5.0.
Incorrect. EMPHASIS-HF showed substantial benefit.
Incorrect. EMPHASIS-HF showed mortality REDUCTION.
Incorrect. Eplerenone is INDICATED in NYHA class II HFrEF based on EMPHASIS-HF.
Incorrect. MR antagonists are recommended in NYHA II–IV HFrEF, not just IV.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman taking spironolactone 50 mg daily for PCOS-related hirsutism is concerned about pregnancy. Which of the following best characterizes the use of spironolactone in pregnancy?
choices: Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy due to teratogenic risk to male fetuses (the antiandrogenic activity of spironolactone can produce feminization of male external genitalia in animal studies; human data are limited but the theoretical risk is concerning). Women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception while taking spironolactone (pregnancy testing prior to starting; combined oral contraceptive often used as both treatment of underlying PCOS AND contraception)
Spironolactone is FDA category A in pregnancy
Spironolactone is the antihypertensive of choice in pregnancy
Spironolactone has no fetal risk
Spironolactone causes only female fetal abnormalities
explanations: Correct. Spironolactone is generally AVOIDED in pregnancy due to its antiandrogenic activity, which has caused feminization of male external genitalia in animal studies (rats given high doses during gestation). Human teratogenicity data are limited but the theoretical risk warrants avoidance. Women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception while taking spironolactone for any indication. For PCOS-related hirsutism, combined oral contraceptive is often paired with spironolactone — providing contraception, additional anti-androgen effect (suppressing ovarian androgen production), and reducing breakthrough bleeding. Pregnancy testing is recommended before starting spironolactone. For pregnancy-related hypertension, methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine are preferred.
Incorrect. Spironolactone is not FDA category A; it is generally avoided in pregnancy.
Incorrect. Methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine are first-line antihypertensives in pregnancy; spironolactone is avoided.
Incorrect. Spironolactone DOES have fetal risk (theoretical antiandrogenic effects on male genitalia).
Incorrect. The principal concern is feminization of MALE external genitalia, not female abnormalities.

questions.stem: A male newborn presents on day 5 of life with severe failure to thrive, dehydration, and salt-wasting. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism)

Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA1) — loss-of-function mutations in ENaC subunits (autosomal recessive, severe multisystem form) or in the mineralocorticoid receptor (autosomal dominant, milder kidney-limited form). The kidney (and sweat glands, intestine in the recessive form) cannot respond to aldosterone — producing severe salt wasting, hyperkalemic acidosis, volume depletion. Aldosterone and renin are HIGH but ineffective. SPIRONOLACTONE WOULD NOT WORK because the lesion is at or distal to the MR. Treatment: salt supplementation, K+ control, careful fluid management
Liddle syndrome
Bartter syndrome
Type 4 RTA from drug therapy
explanations: Incorrect. Conn syndrome features hypertension and hypokalemia; this patient has the OPPOSITE.

Correct. Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA1) is a syndrome of mineralocorticoid resistance. The autosomal recessive form (severe, multisystem) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in ENaC subunits — affecting kidney, sweat glands, and intestine. The autosomal dominant form (milder, kidney-limited) is caused by MR loss-of-function mutations. In both, the kidney cannot respond to aldosterone — Na+ is wasted, K+ is retained, H+ is retained → severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume depletion. Plasma aldosterone and renin are HIGH but INEFFECTIVE. Importantly, SPIRONOLACTONE WOULD NOT WORK because the lesion is at the MR or its downstream channel (ENaC); blocking the MR offers nothing additional. Treatment: aggressive salt supplementation, K+ control (cation exchange resins), careful fluid management, hydrocortisone if there is concurrent adrenal insufficiency. The elevated sweat chloride confirms multisystem ENaC dysfunction (autosomal recessive form).
Incorrect. Liddle features HYPERtension and hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Bartter features hypokalemia, alkalosis, and normal-low BP.
Incorrect. Type 4 RTA from drug therapy is acquired and typically milder; this is a neonatal presentation.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on lisinopril, spironolactone, and ibuprofen develops hyperkalemia and a mild non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Which of the following best characterizes 'type 4 RTA' from drug therapy?
choices: Type 1 (distal) RTA from drug-induced α-intercalated cell dysfunction
Type 2 (proximal) RTA from drug-induced HCO3− wasting

Drug-induced 'type 4 RTA' arises from impaired aldosterone signaling at the principal cell. Reduced aldosterone (or its action) impairs distal Na+ reabsorption and K+/H+ secretion; the result is hyperkalemic mild metabolic acidosis with preserved ability to acidify urine (the H+ secretion machinery itself is intact). Causes include: ACE inhibitors / ARBs (reduced aldosterone), spironolactone / eplerenone (MR antagonism), amiloride / triamterene (ENaC block), heparin (suppressed aldo synthesis), trimethoprim (ENaC block), and many combinations of these. Treatment: discontinue offenders, fludrocortisone in selected cases
Lactic acidosis from drug toxicity
Metabolic alkalosis
explanations: Incorrect. Type 1 RTA features HYPOkalemia; type 4 features HYPERkalemia. The mechanism here is hypoaldosteronism, not α-intercalated cell dysfunction.
Incorrect. Type 2 RTA features hypokalemia and Fanconi syndrome.

Correct. Drug-induced 'type 4 RTA' (hyperkalemic distal RTA from hypoaldosteronism / mineralocorticoid resistance) is common in clinical practice. The mechanism is impaired aldosterone signaling at the collecting duct principal cell — through any of multiple pathways: reduced aldosterone (ACE inhibitors / ARBs / heparin), MR antagonism (spironolactone / eplerenone), or direct ENaC blockade (amiloride / triamterene / trimethoprim). The clinical picture: hyperkalemia, mild non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with normal urine pH (the H+ secretion machinery is intact, but K+ and H+ secretion are coupled — reduced ENaC-driven lumen-negative voltage limits both). Distinguishes from primary type 4 RTA (e.g., diabetic nephropathy with hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism). Management: discontinue or reduce offending agents; fludrocortisone in selected cases.
Incorrect. The clinical picture is hyperkalemic acidosis without elevated anion gap or lactate.
Incorrect. The acidosis is mild metabolic with normal anion gap, not alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man on spironolactone 100 mg daily for resistant HTN has been on it for 4 months and reports new gynecomastia and decreased libido. He asks about the prevalence and management of these effects. Which of the following best characterizes spironolactone's hormonal adverse effects?
choices: These effects are extremely rare (<1%)
These effects are reversible only after a year of discontinuation
These effects are exclusive to women

Spironolactone has well-recognized hormonal adverse effects, particularly at higher doses (≥50 mg/day): gynecomastia (~10% of men at typical HF doses; higher with longer duration and higher doses), decreased libido, impotence, and menstrual irregularities and breast tenderness in women. The mechanism is binding to androgen and progesterone receptors in addition to MR. Management options: switch to eplerenone (highly MR-selective, minimal hormonal effects); use the lowest effective dose; if BP control is the goal, consider alternative classes
These effects only occur in women
explanations: Incorrect. Hormonal effects are not rare; gynecomastia in particular occurs in ~10% of men at HF doses.
Incorrect. Effects are reversible within weeks to months of discontinuation.
Incorrect. Effects affect both men (gynecomastia, decreased libido) and women (menstrual irregularities, breast tenderness).

Correct. Spironolactone's antiandrogen and antiprogesterone activity (from binding androgen and progesterone receptors in addition to MR) produces dose-dependent hormonal adverse effects: in men, gynecomastia (~10% at HF doses; up to 50% at higher doses for resistant HTN), decreased libido, impotence; in women, menstrual irregularities, breast tenderness, mastodynia. Effects are dose- and duration-dependent. Reversible within weeks to months of discontinuation. Management options: (1) switch to eplerenone, which is highly MR-selective and has minimal hormonal activity (preferred when hormonal effects are problematic); (2) use the lowest effective dose; (3) if BP control is the goal, consider alternative drug classes (ARNi, β-blockers, dihydropyridine CCBs).
Incorrect. Hormonal effects affect both men and women.
